chapter.title: Typing Events and Refs
chapter.description: Getting handler and DOM types right without fighting the compiler.

blocks.text: React ships types for every synthetic event. The generic parameter is the element the handler is attached to.
Let inference do the work
An inline handler does not need annotations at all - React's element types already describe the parameter.

blocks.code:
// event is inferred as React.ChangeEvent<HTMLInputElement>
<input onChange={(event) => setValue(event.target.value)} />

blocks.text: target versus currentTarget

items: `currentTarget` is the element the handler is on, and is typed precisely.
`target` is whatever was actually clicked, so it is typed as the more general `EventTarget`.

blocks.text: Prefer `currentTarget` when you need element properties. It avoids the casts that `target` often forces you into.
Common DOM element types

blocks.code:
HTMLInputElement, HTMLTextAreaElement, HTMLSelectElement
HTMLButtonElement, HTMLFormElement, HTMLAnchorElement
HTMLDivElement, HTMLCanvasElement, HTMLVideoElement

blocks.text: useState
TypeScript infers the type from the initial value, which covers most cases. Supply a type argument when the initial value does not describe the full range.
`useState([])` infers `never[]`, so pushing anything into it is an error. Always supply the element type for an empty array.
useRef
The two uses of `useRef` need different types, and the difference matters.
useReducer
Type the state and the action union, and the reducer's exhaustiveness comes free.
With a discriminated union, TypeScript narrows `action` inside each case, so `action.value` is only available where it exists. Miss a case and the return type check catches it.
useContext

blocks.caption: The runtime guard also removes null from the type for every caller.

next.title: Generic Components and Practices
next.description: Components that adapt to their data, and the habits worth keeping.

blocks.text: A component that works with any item type - a list, a table, a select - should be generic rather than typed with `any`.
Useful utility types

blocks.code:
type UserProps = React.ComponentProps<typeof UserCard>;   // borrow a component's props
type PartialUser = Partial<User>;                          // all fields optional
type UserPreview = Pick<User, "id" | "name">;              // a subset
type WithoutId = Omit<User, "id">;                         // everything but id
type Status = "idle" | "loading" | "error";                // a closed set

blocks.text: Practices worth adopting

items: Turn on `strict` in tsconfig. Half the value of TypeScript is in the strict null checks.
Prefer union types over booleans for state: `"idle" | "loading" | "error"` makes invalid combinations unrepresentable.
Avoid `any`. Use `unknown` when a type is genuinely unknown and narrow it before use.
Do not annotate what is already inferred - extra annotations go stale.
Type the boundaries, not the middle: API responses and component props matter most.

blocks.text: `as` is an assertion, not a check. `data as User` tells the compiler to stop asking questions - it does not validate anything. For data from a network, parse it with a schema library such as Zod instead.

blocks.title: Model status as a closed set
blocks.instructions: Complete nextStatus so it returns 'loading' from 'idle', 'idle' from 'loading', and 'idle' from 'error'.
